articles.title: Future of Marketing Briefing: Creators had a big year. Christmas still went to the celebrities
articles.summary: Despite leaning on creators for most of the year, marketers aren’t doing it for the holiday crunch. That job still belongs to celebrities.
articles.excerpt: Join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit Creators are everywhere in marketing these days — everywhere except Christmas ads. The first batch of festive campaigns, from John Lewis, SharkNinja, Ulta Beauty and Burberry among others, makes little for the industry’s favorite obsession. Despite leaning on creators throughout the rest of the year, marketers aren’t doing it for the holiday crunch. That job still belongs to celebrities. Sephora has cast Seth Rogen as a man hopelessly out of his depth, rescued by one of the retailer’s Beauty Advisors before he can do any lasting damage. Over at Kay, Saturday Night Live’s Colin Jost is put through that most well-worn of Christmas tropes: the frantic hunt for the perfect present for someone special. Sports Direct roped in Nike to push the cliche a step further. Its ad follows an uncle wandering the aisles in search of something for his niece, blissfully unaware that a squad of Nike athletes is quietly steering him to the right choice. And Gucci has Mariah Carey — the industry version of the relative who gets passed from house to house every December. This year it’s the luxury brand’s turn to host her. Why these brands do this year after year is no secret. Celebrities, particularly the calibre fronting this year’s crop, are the advertising equivalent of tinsel: nobody calls it innovative but a tree looks bare without it. For CMOs wary of how quickly an ad can set off the internet these days, that familiarity is a safety blanket. John Lewis is the latest case. Within a day of release, its spot had Piers Morgan calling it “possibly the worst advert I’ve ever seen for anything” and Mumsnet testing into the “ungrateful” grandchildren. Dame Kristin Scott Thomas, the ad’s star, escaped without a scratch.

Even with the growth of digital channels such as e-commerce, social and CTV, the physical store remains one of the most influential moments in the path to purchase. According to Grocery TV’s 2026 In-Store Shopper Perception Report , 95% of grocery shoppers make at least half of their purchase decisions in-store. Even younger, in-demand audiences frequent physical retail locations, with 55% of Gen Z consumers shopping in-store at least once a week. Despite this, marketers have historically treated the store more like a retail backdrop than a media channel. Media buyers, especially digital media buyers, have long defaulted to other channels that were easier to tap into. For digital buyers accustomed to unified inventory, real-time optimization and closed-loop attribution, in-store was the opposite: a fragmented, retailer-by-retailer negotiation with no standardized metrics. articles.title: HTML vs. XML Sitemaps for Ecommerce
articles.summary: Both sitemaps help search engines, but neither replaces a fast, well-structured, and well-interlinked website. The post HTML vs. XML Sitemaps for Ecommerce appeared first on Practical Ecommerce .
articles.excerpt: In the web’s early days, developers placed a summary of links to a site’s key sections, such as categories, company pages, policies, and more. The summaries could appear in footers or on standalone pages. Developers called the summaries “sitemaps.” In 2005, Google introduced a new version of sitemaps based on Extensible Markup Language, a 1990s text-based format for storing data, that site owners could submit to Google (via what became Search Console). The aim was to help search engines crawl and index all pages on a site. In time, the industry referred to the versions as “HTML sitemaps” and “XML sitemaps.” XML sitemaps help with discoverability. Search engines can find pages quickly in the sitemap without landing on the site itself. Whether the search-engine bots access and index the newly discovered pages depends on crawl budget, site authority, content relevance, depth and originality , internal linking, and external backlinks, among other signals. Conversely, HTML sitemaps provide no backdoor to a site. Crawlers must land on a site to access an HTML sitemap, likely via internal links. Search engine optimizers disagree on the impact of HTML sitemaps. In my experience, such sitemaps likely help indexing by revealing the internal links to every page. When placed in the footer, HTML sitemaps spread internal link equity to the listed pages. They minimize the number of pages in Search Console’s “ Crawled, currently not indexed ” status. Both sitemaps — HTML and XML — help search engines discover, crawl, and index more pages, especially on larger sites. But neither replaces a website hierarchy that naturally prioritizes important pages. Only a fast, well-structured, and well-interlinked website ensures solid organic search visibility.
